title: Ding-Dong!
paragraphs: When Gran went to stay with her sister for a week, she left her parrot with Omar's family. 'He's no trouble at all,' she promised, handing over a tall cage covered with a blanket. 'He just likes a little chat.' The parrot was grey, with a tail as red as a postbox. He tilted his head and studied Omar with one bright, beady eye.

The next morning, the doorbell rang while Dad was making pancakes. He hurried to the door, still holding the frying pan, but nobody was there. Ten minutes later, the bell rang again. 'Not again!' Dad groaned. Once more, the doorstep was empty.

By lunchtime, Dad had answered the door eleven times. He had peeped through the letterbox and hidden behind the curtains, hoping to catch the prankster, but nobody ever came. Then, as Omar sat doing his homework at the kitchen table, he heard it: a perfect ding-dong, right behind him. He spun round. The parrot was sitting on his perch, looking extremely pleased with himself.

Omar yelled for Dad, who rushed in just in time to see the parrot puff out his chest and go, 'Ding-dong!' In a gruff voice exactly like Dad's, the parrot added, 'Not again!' Dad stared at the cage with his mouth wide open. Then he laughed so hard that he had to sit down.

Over the next few days, the parrot showed off his whole collection of sounds. He copied the ping of the microwave, so Mum kept opening it to find nothing inside. He copied the ring of Dad's phone, so Dad kept searching under the sofa cushions. He even copied Omar's sneeze, which Omar thought was rather rude.

Omar decided that the parrot should learn something useful instead. Every afternoon, he sat beside the cage with a handful of sunflower seeds. 'Welcome home, Gran!' he said, over and over again. The parrot ate every single seed. Then he went, 'Ding-dong!'
On Saturday, Gran came to collect him. The whole family gathered round the cage and held their breath. Gran bent down and smiled. 'Hello, my darling,' she said. 'Did you miss me?'

The parrot fluffed up his feathers, looked her straight in the eye and announced, in Dad's gruffest voice, 'Not again!' For a moment, nobody made a sound. Then Gran began to chuckle, and soon everyone was laughing, even Dad.

As Gran carried the cage down the path to her car, a muffled voice came from under the blanket: 'Welcome home, Gran!' Omar grinned. The parrot had learned it after all, even if his timing was terrible.

questions.prompt:
Look at paragraph 1.
'He tilted his head and **studied** Omar'
Which word is closest in meaning to **studied**?
Tick one.

Look at paragraph 2.
What was Dad making when the doorbell first rang?

Look at paragraph 2.
Find and copy **one** word that shows Dad was fed up.

In paragraphs 2 to 4, Dad's feelings change.
Explain how they change, using evidence from the text.
questions.model: At first, Dad is annoyed because he keeps answering the door and nobody is there. When the bell rings again, he groans, 'Not again!' When he finds out that the parrot has been making the noise, he is amazed and then thinks it is funny. He 'stared at the cage with his mouth wide open' and then 'laughed so hard that he had to sit down'.
points: Explains that at first Dad is annoyed or fed up, with evidence, e.g. 'Not again!' Dad groaned.
Explains that when he finds out about the parrot he is amazed or amused, with evidence, e.g. he 'laughed so hard that he had to sit down'.

questions.prompt:
Look at paragraph 5.
'the parrot showed off his whole collection of sounds'
What does this suggest about the parrot?
Tick one.
options: He could make lots of different sounds and was proud of them.
He kept a box of noisy toys in his cage.
He only knew how to make one sound.
He was too shy to make any noise.

questions.prompt:
Look at paragraph 6.
What did Omar have with him when he sat beside the cage?

Look at paragraph 9.
'The parrot had learned it after all, even if his timing was terrible.'
Why was the parrot's timing terrible?
questions.model: He said 'Welcome home, Gran!' just as Gran was leaving with him, instead of when she arrived. When she arrived, he said 'Not again!'
points: explaining that the parrot said 'Welcome home, Gran!' when Gran was leaving (not when she arrived), or that he said 'Not again!' when she arrived.

questions.prompt:
The words 'Not again!' appear in paragraphs 2, 4 and 8.
Why do you think the writer repeats them?
Tick one.
options: To build up to a joke: the parrot learns Dad's words and then says them to Gran.
To show that Dad says 'Not again!' whenever he is happy.
To show that Gran is cross with the parrot.
To tell the reader how to teach a parrot to talk.

questions.prompt: Using information from the text, tick one box in each row to show whether each statement is **true** or **false**.
statements: Gran went to stay with her sister for a week.
Dad caught a prankster hiding behind the curtains.
The parrot copied the sound of Omar's sneeze.
Gran came to collect the parrot on Sunday.

questions.prompt:
Give **two** impressions of Gran's parrot.
Use evidence from the text to support your answer.
questions.model: The parrot is clever, because he can copy the doorbell, the microwave, Dad's phone and even Dad's voice. He is also cheeky, because he fooled Dad into answering the door eleven times and then looked 'extremely pleased with himself'.
points: each different impression that is backed up with evidence from the text (1 mark each), such as:
clever or good at copying: he copies the doorbell, the microwave, Dad's phone, Omar's sneeze and Dad's voice
cheeky or mischievous: Dad answered the door eleven times, and the parrot looked 'extremely pleased with himself'
a show-off: he 'showed off his whole collection of sounds' and puffed out his chest

questions.prompt:
Which is the best summary of the whole story?
Tick one.
options: A parrot fools a family by copying sounds, and then surprises Gran when she comes to collect him.
A family buys a parrot, but it will not make a single sound.
Dad catches a prankster who keeps ringing his doorbell.
Gran teaches her parrot to say 'Welcome home, Gran!' while she is away.

questions.prompt:
At the end of the story, Gran takes the parrot home.
What do you think the parrot will do at Gran's house?
Use evidence from the text to support your prediction.
questions.model: I think the parrot will play tricks on Gran by copying the sounds in her house, such as her doorbell or her phone, because at Omar's house he copied 'the ping of the microwave' and 'the ring of Dad's phone'. He will probably say 'Welcome home, Gran!' at the wrong moments too, because 'his timing was terrible'.
points: a sensible prediction (1 mark), e.g. he will copy the sounds in Gran's house and trick her; he will say 'Welcome home, Gran!' at the wrong times; he will say 'Not again!' in Dad's voice.
evidence from the text that supports the prediction (1 mark), e.g. he copied the doorbell, the microwave and Dad's phone; he learned 'Welcome home, Gran!', but 'his timing was terrible'.

questions.prompt: Number these events 1 to 5 in the order they happen in the story.
items: Dad laughs so hard that he has to sit down.
Gran hands over the parrot's cage.
A voice says 'Welcome home, Gran!' from under the blanket.
Dad answers the door holding a frying pan.
Omar tries to teach the parrot to say 'Welcome home, Gran!'
